summary: A steel-towered light at the end of Manistique's east breakwater, lit in 1914 and 1916, automated in 1969 and now privately owned.

structures.note: Riveted steel tower, square pyramidal; 34 ft to lantern centre (USLHS); 50 ft above water. Diaphone on the third floor (Bureau description, via LighthouseFriends).
Two sets of quarters on Range Street (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Light and dwelling privately owned (LighthouseFriends, 2013 sale); grounds open, tower and dwelling closed; walk out along the breakwater from Lakeview Park.

facts.agency: Private owner since the 2013 General Services Administration auction (LighthouseFriends; check current owner)

events.note: Temporary fixed red light (45 candlepower) suspended from a pole to mark the west end of the new east breakwater (LighthouseFriends)
Congress provides $20,000 for aids to navigation in Manistique Harbor (22 October 1913)

25 ft steel skeletal tower with acetylene light established on the west breakwater, 30 October 1914 (LighthouseFriends); Bulletin 1914 lists 'Manistique Harbor, Mich.' among lights established (two lens lanterns, one oil and one acetylene)
Steel tower and duplex keepers' dwelling completed
East breakwater light transferred to the new structure, 17 August 1916
USLHS: original optic fourth-order Fresnel, 1916. LighthouseFriends: 300 mm lens lantern in 1916
Fourth-order lens replaced the lens lantern (LighthouseFriends); conflicts with the USLHS 1916 date
Secretary commends keeper Charles E. Corlett and assistant William Renier for valuable assistance (11 January 1918); the notice describes no rescue
Radiobeacon established at the station at the opening of navigation
Automated the year after the car ferry and railroad ceased (1968)
Officially disestablished as a manned unit, 30 August 1969
Fourth-order lens removed from the tower; now at Wisconsin Maritime Museum
NRHP asset record (NRIS 05000980), published 6 September 2005; the sources read do not give a separate listing date
Light made available under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act (15 May 2012)
GSA online auction (closed 15 July 2013); only bid $15,000 from a private buyer in Ohio

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends dates the first light, a temporary red light at the west end of the new east breakwater, to 1912; USLHS gives 1913 as the year established and the 1914 Bulletin lists lights established in Manistique Harbor. The permanent tower dates from 1916 (USLHS, LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends 1912 (temporary light at the east breakwater, the first light on the site); USLHS 1913 (year established); Bulletin 1914 (lights established in Manistique Harbor, including a west-breakwater tower). The story gives the sequence: temporary light 1912, appropriation October 1913, west-breakwater tower October 1914, permanent tower and transfer 1916.
Original optic: USLHS fourth-order in 1916; LighthouseFriends 300 mm lens lantern in 1916 and a fourth-order lens from 1918. Not resolved; the story gives both.

The Board's 1892 request (for $32,000) is for a light on Pointe aux Barques; the 1893 report records a coast light and fog signal at Manistique authorized by the act of 15 February 1893 at not more than $32,000; the 1899 report files the unfunded proposal as 'Pointe aux Barques (Manistique)'. The reports do not say whether these are one proposal; the story says so.

notes_for_editor: Unverified: the station record's characteristic Iso R 6s and 9 m range were not checked against the Light List. The record's fog signal 'horn' conflicts with the Bureau description (diaphone) quoted by LighthouseFriends. The record's 1913 first_lit conflicts with LighthouseFriends (temporary light 1912) and the 1914 Bulletin entry; the proposed correction is to 1914. The record's 11.0 m tower height is not the USLHS figure (34 ft to lantern, 10.4 m). The 1918 fourth-order lens date (LighthouseFriends) conflicts with the 1916 date (USLHS). The NRHP nomination PDF is not digitised (placeholder). The owner (2013 buyer, Bill Collins) is from LighthouseFriends; the sources read stop at 2013 and the current owner and access must be checked before publication. The 1899 'Pointe aux Barques (Manistique)' heading is a different proposal from the 1893 Manistique authorization; the story keeps them apart. The Chronicling America search for 1912-1916 Michigan papers returned nothing. The 1918 commendation gives keeper Corlett and assistant Renier; the bulletin's OCR garbles the sentence, so only the opening phrase is quoted. Keepers from the USLHS roster (39 lines, including a Coast Guard heading from 1959). Roster lines with 'at least' carry from_approx or to_approx flags. No woman keeper appears in the sources read. Fact-check pass 2026-10-22: the 1918 commendation text is OCR-garbled after 'valuable assistance'; a Red Cross recruiting detail in the same sentence cannot be read reliably, so the story omits it. The 1918 Bulletin issue text mentions events of 10 and 15 January 1918, so the commendation's year is 1918. The 1913 Bulletin is cited at the uslhs.org URL that corpus.py prints (LighthouseServiceBulletin_1913_0.pdf). LighthouseFriends' sentence that 'a lighthouse was finally built in the gap between Poverty Island and Seul Choix Point' after Manistique harbor work is not tied by the sources read to the east breakwater light, which stands at the river mouth; the story does not link them. The LighthouseFriends 'Augsut' typo is kept inside the quotation as printed. Shape: the story has five chapters at about 980 words, one more than the moderate-length shape allows; the Storms, wrecks and rescues chapter was removed because the only dated service item (the 1918 commendation) is not a rescue and is now in The keepers.
